prompt: In the proof of the extreme value theorem, why must the domain be compact?
answer: So that a limit of points in the domain stays in the domain
options: So that a limit of points in the domain stays in the domain
So that f is monotone on the domain, which the proof needs to choose a maximising point
So that the plot has enough pixels
So that f is differentiable
explanation: A maximising sequence has a convergent subsequence (boundedness) whose limit lies in the set (closedness). Continuity then carries the maximum value to that point.
hint: Where does the limit of the maximising sequence live?

prompt: f is continuous and one-to-one on a compact set K. Is the inverse f⁻¹ continuous on f(K)?
answer: Yes: compactness makes f a closed map, so the inverse is continuous
options: Yes: compactness makes f a closed map, so the inverse is continuous
No: compactness is irrelevant here, so a continuous one-to-one map can have a discontinuous inverse
Yes, if f is increasing on the set
Yes, if K is an interval of the line
explanation: Closed subsets of K are compact, so their images are compact and hence closed. So preimages of closed sets under f⁻¹ are closed, and f⁻¹ is continuous.
